tagline: Shell Canyon switchbacks lead to granite heights and a gentler eastern descent
intro: US 14 crosses the Bighorns on a paved, two-lane road, climbing western switchbacks before descending more gradually toward Dayton. Wyoming’s Transportation Commission adopted 47 miles between Shell and Dayton as the Big Horn Scenic Byway. The tourism office describes a drive past forests, meadows, waterfalls and deep canyons. WYDOT gives approximately an hour as the minimum driving time, with stops taking longer. Along Shell Canyon, cottonwoods and willows give way at higher elevations to slopes dominated by juniper and sagebrush.

The highway number once took a different course across the mountains. Before 1940, US 14 ran through Lovell and Powell on the route now signed US 14A. In 1940 it took over Wyoming 520 between Greybull and Burgess Junction, bringing the US 14 designation to the Shell Canyon crossing. The older route became Wyoming 14 and, after confusion over the names, US 14A in 1965.

Starting from Shell, the designated stretch begins around four miles from town at the national forest boundary. The road squeezes through Shell Canyon, where the creek sometimes disappears from view far below. Shell Falls and Granite Creek come before 9,033-foot Granite Pass. Continue through Burgess Junction, then descend toward the overlook at Fallen City, 6.5 miles west of Dayton.

moments.title: Shell Falls
moments.text: Shell Creek drops 120 feet over granite at Shell Falls, on the north side of the highway. The falls expose a much longer story in the surrounding rock. From the rest area and interpretive center, Cambrian sandstone, about 550 million years old, can be seen resting on Precambrian rock 2.9 billion years old. Copman’s Tomb, a large limestone promontory, is visible to the north. Wyoming’s tourism account describes nature trails and interpretive signs accompanying the waterfall. Downstream, the town of Shell takes its name from the abundance of fossil shells found in the area.
moments.notice: Look for sandstone resting on much older Precambrian rock near the falls.

moments.title: Granite Creek
moments.text: A tornado crossed Granite Creek in 1959, leaving damaged trees on the opposite mountain. WYDOT’s 2000 brochure describes an interpretive sign at the picnic area explaining the damage. It also notes that trees recover slowly in this environment and at this elevation.

moments.title: Fallen City
moments.text: Fallen City is a field of Madison limestone blocks that toppled onto the rock below. The Forest Service places the formation’s story in the uplift of the Bighorn Mountains, when faults and fractures developed in the rock. WYDOT describes the overlook at the national forest boundary, 6.5 miles west of Dayton, as a place to see both these blocks and the Powder River Basin beyond. This boundary marks the official eastern end of the designated drive. The road’s eastern descent from Granite Pass is steadier and less steep than the switchback climb through the western canyon.

practical: Shell Falls: WYDOT notes that heavy snow can briefly close the byway in winter or early spring. (checked 2026-10-11)
